advantages: Explains why each mechanism in the unit exists, so the mechanisms can be compared on one axis - what scarce resource buys agreement - instead of being memorised as a list.
Gives the three-property vocabulary (agreement, validity, termination) that lets you diagnose what a proposed mechanism actually guarantees.
Frames the fault model, which is the difference between crash tolerance and Byzantine tolerance and therefore between an academic protocol and one usable against an attacker.
limitations: The comparison is a framework, not a choice: it does not pick a mechanism for a given business, which is what a business-model course ultimately asks.
Naming a scarce resource does not quantify the cost - the actual price of security per transaction depends on network parameters and token price, not on the mechanism alone.
Introduction to Consensus Methods.memoryTrick: **Agreement, Validity, Termination — A.V.T. And every mechanism spends something scarce.**

examAnswer.question: What is a consensus mechanism, what properties must it deliver, and what does each mechanism spend? (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
A consensus mechanism is the rule by which a network of independent, mutually distrusting nodes agrees on one ordered history of transactions without any central authority telling them what to accept.

**The problem it solves.** A single server keeps one ledger because it is in one place. A blockchain splits that ledger across thousands of machines, so it inherits the classic distributed-systems failure: a node may crash, be slow, or actively lie, and yet every honest node must end up with the same transaction order. If they do not, there is no ledger - only thousands of contradictory claims. A blockchain with an operator who can simply declare the truth has no need for any of this machinery.

**The three properties any protocol must deliver.** Agreement: no two honest nodes decide differently about the same block. Validity: only blocks whose transactions satisfy the rules are accepted - a node cannot decide on an invalid block even if all its peers agree. Termination: the protocol always makes progress and never deadlocks, regardless of the messages that are delayed or dropped.

**The fault model.** Nodes can fail in three ways. Crash faults mean a node stops; omission faults mean it stays silent; Byzantine faults mean a node lies, forges signatures, or colludes with other nodes. Tolerating crashes only is not enough for an open network, because an attacker is not a crashed node - it is a crashed node that also talks. Byzantine fault tolerance is therefore the target.

**What each mechanism spends.** Every mechanism buys agreement with a scarce resource, and that resource is the real running cost of the ledger. Proof of Work spends electricity and specialised hardware, so the cost is paid continuously and burned. Proof of Stake spends capital that is locked and can be destroyed, so the cost is paid by the owners of value and is recoverable in the sense that honest behaviour keeps the stake earning. Proof of Burn spends tokens outright, permanently reducing supply. Proof of Activity spends both work and stake. Proof of Elapsed Time spends trust in a hardware vendor rather than any resource of its own. Simplified Byzantine Fault Tolerance spends the overhead of a known, small membership running two voting rounds per decision, and in exchange buys deterministic finality.

**The consequence.** The choice of mechanism therefore determines who can join (permissionless mechanisms need economic rewards; permissioned ones need an admission list), what the failure mode is (wasted electricity versus slashed stake versus a backdoored chip), and what the business can promise its customers - probabilistic finality in hours, as with Bitcoin, or deterministic finality in seconds, as with an SBFT network. In a business-models course this is the point: the consensus mechanism sets the cost structure that the rest of the business model has to live inside.

advantages: The security cost is priced in a resource external to the token - electricity and hardware - so an attacker cannot inflate their own defences by printing more coins.
Verification is almost free for anyone: checking a hash against the target costs one double SHA-256, so full nodes need no stake and no permission.
The chain with the most accumulated work is objectively the real chain, so the rule for resolving a fork needs no committee and no voting.
History is expensive to rewrite, so a confirmed transaction is very hard to reverse - the property the original double-spending problem needed.
limitations: Enormous energy consumption for a security budget that buys only probabilistic finality; the electricity is destroyed every block.
It excludes ordinary participants - specialised mining hardware and cheap power are now a barrier to entry.
Hash power can be rented and concentrated, so a mining pool or a nation-state can buy influence on the order of its spend.
Finality is probabilistic: six confirmations are a strong probability, not a guarantee, and a business cannot put a non-reversible settlement on it without accepting a reorganisation risk.
Proof of Work (PoW).memoryTrick: **PoW = burn electricity to guess a hash. Target down, difficulty up. Attacker must outspend, not outrun.**
Proof of Work (PoW).modernNote: Bitcoin still runs PoW, but the energy argument has changed the landscape: the network's annualised energy use is now comparable to that of a mid-sized country, and the search for cheaper verification has pushed the industry towards proof of stake and towards energy-efficient consensus. Read the syllabus's PoW as the historical reference point and the modern context as the reason PoS exists.

examAnswer.question: Explain Proof of Work with the target/difficulty rule, the nonce search, the 51% attack and the cost of mounting it. (15 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Proof of Work is a consensus mechanism in which a miner repeatedly varies a nonce in the block header and hashes until the resulting hash falls below a shared target, so the right to produce the next block is bought with electricity and hardware rather than granted by anyone.

**The problem it solves.** Bitcoin needed a ledger with no trusted server. Any scheme based only on software statements would be captured by whoever wrote the most nodes, so PoW made forgery expensive by making computation itself the scarce resource. Rewriting history means redoing all the work, so an attacker must outspend the honest network, not merely outpace it.

**How it works, in order.**
1. *Block assembly.* The miner collects pending transactions into a candidate block and builds the header, which carries the previous block hash, the Merkle root of the transactions, a timestamp, the compact target nBits, and a 32-bit nonce field.
2. *The target and validity rule.* Every node shares one 256-bit target value encoded in nBits. A block is valid only if the hash of its header is numerically less than that target - equivalently, if it has the right number of leading zero bits.
3. *The nonce search.* The miner sets the nonce, computes the double SHA-256 of the 80-byte header, and if the digest is above the target increments the nonce and hashes again. It repeats until the hash lands under the target. Against a 64-bit target this takes roughly 2^64 hashes on average, and the 2^32 nonce space is exhausted and restarted using extraNonce in the coinbase.
4. *Difficulty retargeting.* Every 2016 blocks - about 14 days at 10 minutes per block - the network recomputes the target from the actual timestamps of those blocks, so the average block time stays near 10 minutes and difficulty rises automatically as hardware improves.
5. *Broadcast and verification.* The winning header and block are broadcast. Every receiving node recomputes the double hash and checks it against nBits, the target and the PoW limit, rejecting the block if any check fails.
6. *Chain extension and reward.* The valid block is appended to the chain with the most accumulated work, and the miner collects the block subsidy plus transaction fees.

**The 51% attack.** An attacker controlling more than half the total hash rate can mine a conflicting chain faster than the honest network, and thereby double-spend coins or censor transactions. What the attacker cannot do is change the contents of transactions, forge signatures or take keys. The point of the number is not that 51% is impossible but that it is priced: to maintain the fork the attacker must keep buying hash power and keep burning electricity for every block of it, while the honest network's expected work per block is 2^64 hashes. The attacker's outlay therefore exceeds the value of the chain it is trying to replace - unless the chain's total hash power is small, which is exactly the case on some altcoins where such attacks have actually happened.

**Consequence.** The security budget of the whole network is the total electricity spent per block. That budget is what pays honest miners to keep hashing and validating, and it is the number that eventually has to come from transaction fees once the subsidy ends. Every other weakness of PoW - waste, exclusion of ordinary participants, probabilistic rather than deterministic finality - follows from this one design choice: make computation the price of trust.

advantages: Energy use collapses from PoW levels to the electricity of a validator node, so the security budget becomes orders of magnitude cheaper per transaction.
The thing at risk is the network's own token, so the cost of an attack scales with the value the attacker would destroy - a self-correcting price.
Misbehaviour can be punished directly by slashing, which PoW cannot do at all.
Modern designs add deterministic finality, so a block once confirmed can never be reversed even by a large share of stake.
Participation needs no specialised hardware: a modest machine and 32 ETH are enough, which is far less exclusionary than mining.
limitations: Stake concentrates over time, so control tends to move toward large holders and validators, which raises governance questions a business must answer.
Security depends entirely on the slashing rules being able to detect and punish equivocation; an unpunished attack is free.
Long-range and weak-subjectivity attacks are new weaknesses that PoW does not have, and they force a social recovery rule into the protocol.
Validators must be online and capital is locked, so there is an opportunity cost and an availability cost.
The 33% reorganisation threshold is a much smaller share of the network than a 51% hash majority, so PoS tolerates less adversarial capital than its PoW counterpart.
Proof of Stake (PoS).memoryTrick: **PoS = stake, not fuel. Vote twice: prepare and commit. Slashing kills nothing-at-stake. Two thirds stake = final.**
Proof of Stake (PoS).modernNote: Proof of stake has moved from theory to the default for major networks: Ethereum moved to PoS with the Merge in 2022, and most newer large chains use PoS. The mechanics in the syllabus - 32 ETH minimum stake, attestations, slashing for double-signing, two-thirds supermajority finality - describe Ethereum's Casper FFG family of rules. Where the syllabus says 'selection weighted by stake', the real protocol adds pseudo-random shuffling so a validator cannot simply wait for its turn to collude.

examAnswer.question: Explain Proof of Stake: validator selection by stake, slashing, the nothing-at-stake and long-range attacks, and deterministic finality. (15 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Proof of Stake is a consensus mechanism in which validators lock capital as stake and are selected to propose and attest to blocks roughly in proportion to that stake, so control of the network is bought with locked, slashable capital rather than burned electricity.

**The problem it solves.** PoW proves a miner spent electricity. That is verifiable, but it is wasteful and it excludes anyone without mining hardware and cheap power. PoS replaces the burnt resource with something the network already needs and that participants actually care about - the coin itself. Control is then proportional to economic commitment, energy use collapses, and dishonesty can be punished directly instead of merely being unprofitable.

**How it works, in order.**
1. *Staking and bonding.* A validator locks at least 32 ETH as stake. More stake means more influence. The deposit is collateral that the protocol is able to burn.
2. *Slot and committee selection.* Time is divided into 12-second slots. For each slot the protocol selects one proposer and an attestation committee, with selection weighted by effective stake (and pseudo-randomised, so a validator cannot simply wait for a favourable slot).
3. *Block proposal.* The proposer gathers transactions, builds the block and broadcasts it with a proposal for the committee.
4. *Attestation and finality.* Committee members sign attestations for the block. When attestations carrying at least two thirds of the staked ETH are collected for a checkpoint, that checkpoint is finalised and can never be reversed.
5. *Slashing for equivocation.* A validator that is provably caught signing two conflicting blocks - double-signing - or surrounding itself with contradictory votes has part of its 32 ETH burned and is ejected from the validator set.
6. *Rewards and penalties.* Honest, online attestation earns a small reward; downtime loses part of the reward and repeated downtime is penalised, so availability has a price too.

**Slashing and nothing-at-stake.** Slashing is the mechanism that makes PoS honest. Without it, a validator could sign two competing blocks at no extra cost: a losing signature earns nothing and costs nothing. That is the nothing-at-stake problem - the attacker's expected cost of equivocating is zero, so the honest chain is not safe. Slashing makes the dishonest path visibly expensive by burning the stake, which is why provable evidence of equivocation is the trigger. In PoW the analogous double work is priced automatically, because the attacker's second chain costs real electricity.

**Long-range attacks.** Nothing-at-stake is not the whole story. A validator who unbonds long ago and is no longer slashable can re-use that stake to build an alternative history of a weakly finalised chain, so the attack cannot be punished after the fact. Defences are slashing conditions that require validators to signal their stake is still live, and a social recovery rule - the community simply decides the correct chain - which is a governance mechanism smuggled into the protocol.

**Deterministic finality.** Modern PoS adds a rule that probabilistic finality could not give: once a checkpoint has been attested by a supermajority of stake, that block cannot be reversed even by an attacker controlling a large fraction of the stake. This is what distinguishes a chain with genuine finality from one where a block can be reorganised after the fact.

**The thresholds.** Roughly 33% of staked value is enough to reorganise a weakly finalised chain; about 66% is needed to break finality outright - which is why the two-thirds attestation rule is set where it is.

**Consequence.** PoS buys the same agreement as PoW with capital at risk instead of electricity burnt, so the security budget per transaction falls by orders of magnitude. The price is a new set of dependencies: the slashing rules must be sound, stake concentration must be watched, and the long-range and weak-subjectivity issues must be handled by an explicit social rule.

advantages: No mining hardware and no pre-existing stake are required, so a brand-new chain can bootstrap security from nothing.
The commitment is final: burnt tokens can never be redeemed, so there is no unlock date after which a participant can walk away.
Destruction is deflationary, which some designs use deliberately as a value mechanism rather than merely a cost.
The proof is a normal on-chain transaction, so it is verifiable by anyone without extra infrastructure.
limitations: The cost is unrecoverable, so a participant's capital is genuinely gone - participation is a purchase, not a deposit.
Burning concentrates wealth among those who burned earliest and burned most, so it can be captured in the same way as any other scarce resource.
It does not by itself decide who produces blocks; it is usually a weighting or access layer over another consensus rule.
The mechanism is deflationary by construction, which is a liability for use cases that need a stable money supply.
Proof of Burn (PoB).memoryTrick: **PoB = the receipt is the proof. Send to an unspendable address; supply falls forever.**

examAnswer.question: What is Proof of Burn, what does a participant actually do, and why is it useful for bootstrapping a new chain? (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Proof of Burn is a consensus mechanism in which a participant demonstrates commitment by sending tokens to an address that provably cannot spend them, so the cost of participation is permanently destroyed rather than rented as locked capital or burnt electricity.

**The problem it solves.** A new chain has no history, no mining hardware and no pre-existing stake to secure it, but every chain needs a scarce value that a newcomer can acquire and consume. PoB answers this by making the participant destroy value outright. The burnt tokens are removed from total supply and can never be redeemed, so the commitment is final rather than temporary - which is the crucial difference from PoS, where the stake is only at risk.

**What a participant actually does, in order.**
1. *Burn.* The participant sends tokens to a burn address whose private key is provably absent, or to an output script with no known spend path, so the tokens can never move again.
2. *Supply destruction.* The tokens leave circulation immediately and total supply falls. This is not a lock-up with an unlock date - there is no path back.
3. *Receipt as proof.* The burn transaction itself is the proof of commitment. There is no separate certificate to trust: every node verifies the destruction by reading the transaction chain.
4. *Weighing up.* A participant who burns to several addresses, or burns more, increases the probability of being selected to produce blocks, so competition is priced by the quantity destroyed.
5. *Competing.* After burning, the participant competes exactly like a PoW miner or a PoS validator and receives the block reward if it wins.

**Why it is good for bootstrapping.** PoET-like hardware is unnecessary and PoS-like pre-existing stake is unnecessary - a newcomer can buy tokens on an open market, burn them, and enter. This makes it the natural mechanism for launching a chain that has to create its own security from nothing.

**Advantages and limitations.** The advantages are that the commitment is irrefutable, that the proof is a plain transaction, and that the destruction is deflationary by construction. The limitations are that the capital is unrecoverable, that burning concentrates value in the earliest and largest burners, that the mechanism does not on its own determine who produces blocks, and that a deflationary supply is a liability for applications needing stable money.

**Consequence.** PoB is best understood not as a competitor to PoW or PoS but as a way of manufacturing a committed membership out of nothing - it is frequently used as an access or weighting layer while the actual block production is run by another consensus rule.

advantages: Keeps PoW's resistance to a cheap 51% hash attack, so grinding the hash lottery still matters.
Adds PoS's cheap, near-instant finality, so a confirmed block does not need many confirmations.
Requires both work and economic commitment to activate a block, so neither a hash-power majority nor a stake majority alone can force a fork through.
A fork that loses the staking contest forfeits the stake, so the losing side is punished economically as well as in wasted work.
limitations: It inherits the weaknesses of both parents: the waste of PoW and the concentration and long-range issues of PoS.
The staking step adds latency and a failure mode - a block that is mined but never staked is wasted work.
The rule set is harder to reason about than either parent, which matters for governance and for a business promising a predictable protocol.
It is now largely of historical interest, since the networks that mattered most moved either to pure PoS or to other designs.
Proof of Activity (PoA).memoryTrick: **PoA = mine, then stake, then confirm. Work alone does not activate a block.**
Proof of Activity (PoA).modernNote: In this course Proof of Activity is the PoW-plus-PoS hybrid. It is not Proof of Authority - that is the separate permissioned mechanism where named validators hold fixed voting weight, and conflating the two is the classic error in this unit.

examAnswer.question: Explain Proof of Activity as a PoW-plus-PoS hybrid, including the stake-confirmation step and what happens when the stake is not confirmed, and distinguish it from pure PoW and pure PoS. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Proof of Activity is a hybrid consensus mechanism in which a block is mined by proof of work but only becomes active once its miner stakes the block reward and that stake is confirmed by the other miners. Note carefully: in this syllabus Proof of Activity is the PoW-plus-PoS hybrid - mine, then stake-confirm. It is not Proof of Authority, which is the permissioned mechanism in which a named set of validators holds fixed voting weight.

**The problem it solves.** Pure PoW inherits PoW's waste and its probabilistic finality: the chain with the most burnt electricity wins, and finality is a probability rather than a guarantee. Pure PoS inherits the risk that stake is concentrated and that the long-range and weak-subjectivity attacks exist at all. PoA keeps the PoW mining step as a lottery against cheap majority attacks, and adds a stake-confirmation step, so the chain with real economic commitment wins - not merely the chain with the most electricity burnt.

**How it works, in order.**
1. *Mine by proof of work.* Miners still run the full PoW nonce search to produce a candidate block. The work step is not removed, only supplemented.
2. *Stake the reward.* To make the block active, the miner must additionally send or lock the block reward as stake. Producing a block becomes a two-step commitment rather than one.
3. *Confirmation vote.* Miners then vote on which stake-bearing chain is valid, comparing the accumulated work and the staked value of the competing chains.
4. *Activation and finality.* Once a block is staked and confirmed by a supermajority of stake, it becomes active and final. Work alone finalises nothing.
5. *Fork attrition.* A fork that stops being staked loses the network's confidence, and its stakers lose their stake - so hash power alone cannot win a fork.
6. *Inherited properties.* The chain keeps PoW's resistance to a cheap 51% hash attack and gains PoS's cheap, near-instant finality, without being purely either.

**If the stake is not confirmed.** The block never becomes active and is effectively orphaned; the mining work is wasted and the miner gains nothing from it. On a fork, the chain that stops being staked loses the network's confidence even if it holds more accumulated work - so the accumulated work alone is not the tie-breaker, and an attacker with a hash majority cannot push a fork through without stake to match.

**Contrast with pure PoW.** In pure PoW the chain with the most accumulated work is final on its own, and an attacker with majority hash power can finalise a conflicting chain. In PoA that is not enough: the block must be staked and confirmed, so the attacker's fork dies for lack of stake.

**Contrast with pure PoS.** In pure PoS there is no work at all, so the grinding that makes a cheap 51% hash attack expensive is absent. PoA keeps that step deliberately, which is the entire reason the hybrid exists.

**Consequence.** PoA is the compromise that was proposed while it was unclear whether PoS would work in practice: it keeps the well-understood, adversarially-tested properties of PoW and adds the cheap finality of PoS. Its cost is that the protocol is harder to reason about and inherits both parents' weaknesses.

advantages: Near-zero resource consumption - a node waits rather than burns electricity or locks capital.
Very fast: the block interval is set by the wait, so finality arrives in seconds with no probabilistic confirmation period.
Deterministic finality in a permissioned setting, which is what enterprise users are buying.
Simple to state and to implement compared with a full voting protocol.
limitations: It replaces computational trust with hardware-vendor trust: a backdoored or compromised TEE breaks the randomness and therefore the whole protocol.
It is only suitable for permissioned networks with a known, small membership - it cannot bootstrap an open network.
It relies on an external attestation infrastructure that must itself be available and trusted.
The lottery makes leadership random, which is poor for workloads that want a stable, named validator set, and it wastes waiting time that is not useful work.
Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET).memoryTrick: **PoET = the raffle inside the sealed machine. Shortest wait wins, TEE signs the ticket.**
Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET).modernNote: PoET was Intel's proposal for a consortium chain and was never adopted at scale by a major public network; permissioned ledgers in practice tend to use PBFT-style voting or Raft/Paxos instead. Treat it in the exam as the canonical TEE-based consensus, and note the trust assumption explicitly.

examAnswer.question: Explain Proof of Elapsed Time, its trusted-execution-environment basis and the trust assumption it makes. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Proof of Elapsed Time is a permissioned consensus mechanism in which each participant waits a randomly chosen period inside a trusted execution environment, and the participant whose wait expires first wins the right to produce the next block. It is a lottery, not a computation.

**The problem it solves.** In a small permissioned network there is no need for the enormous waste of PoW, but there is still a need to pick one leader per round without a central party assigning the role. PoET replaces computational search with pure waiting - but waiting alone is worthless unless the random wait is genuinely unpredictable, because otherwise any node could simply claim the shortest wait. So the randomness is delegated to a trusted execution environment, and the cost of the mechanism is moved from electricity to hardware trust.

**How it works, in order.**
1. *Random wait generation.* Each participant asks the TEE for a random wait time that the other participants cannot see or predict in advance.
2. *TEE attestation.* The TEE runs inside hardware isolation such as Intel SGX, and signs the wait value together with a certificate proving that the wait was genuinely random and unobserved.
3. *Certificate verification.* The other nodes verify the TEE's signature and the validity of the certificate before accepting that participant's wait.
4. *Shortest wait wins.* When the waits expire, the participant with the lowest wait value - the one whose timer ran out first - is granted the right to produce the next block.
5. *Proposal and finality.* The winner proposes the block. In a small, known validator set the block is confirmed almost immediately, giving near-instant finality.
6. *Next round.* A fresh round starts immediately with new waits from every participant, so nobody can monopolise the leader role.

**The trust assumption.** Security rests on the TEE vendor and its attestation infrastructure. If the chip, the firmware or the attestation service is compromised, the randomness is controlled by an attacker and the protocol's leader selection fails. This is a deliberate exchange: the network trades computational trust for hardware-vendor trust, and in exchange gets near-instant deterministic finality at almost no running cost. That is a reasonable deal for a consortium of known institutions trading on a shared ledger, and an unreasonable one for an open network - which is why PoET is a permissioned mechanism by design.

**Consequence.** PoET is the clearest example in the unit of the general principle that every consensus mechanism buys agreement with a specific scarce resource: electricity for PoW, capital for PoS, destroyed tokens for PoB, and vendor trust for PoET.

advantages: Deterministic finality: a committed decision can never be reversed, so a business can settle on the chain rather than on a probability.
Fast: two voting rounds give finality in seconds instead of hours of confirmations.
No wasted resource - no electricity is burnt, so the running cost is a fraction of PoW's.
The safety proof is clean: the 3f+1 bound and the 2f+1 quorum guarantee any two quorums overlap in an honest node, so conflicting blocks cannot both commit.
Known membership means identity and admission are controlled, which suits regulated business use.
limitations: Every transaction costs several network rounds of voting, so throughput is far lower than a probabilistic chain.
It scales badly with membership: the number of messages grows with the square of the node count, so it suits tens of nodes, not thousands.
There is no economic incentive - no block reward - so nodes must be run for other reasons, and a node that stops participating is a liveness problem the view change has to absorb.
The committee is known and small, so it introduces a governance and trust surface that a permissionless chain does not have.
Simplified Byzantine Fault Tolerance.memoryTrick: **SBFT = 3f+1 nodes, 2f+1 quorum, two rounds (prepare, commit), then done forever.**

examAnswer.question: Explain SBFT: the leader-based voting rounds, the quorum sizes, the 3f+1 bound with a worked computation, and the finality guarantee. (15 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Simplified Byzantine Fault Tolerance is a leader-based voting protocol in which a leader proposes an ordered request, the replicas broadcast prepare and commit votes, and the decision becomes final once 2f+1 commit votes are collected - with at least 3f+1 replicas required in total to tolerate f Byzantine nodes.

**The problem it solves.** Permissioned networks cannot rely on the probabilistic finality of PoW, because a business cannot run its settlement on a block that might be reversed tomorrow. SBFT replaces the probabilistic race with an explicit voting protocol: an honest majority of a known membership signs off, the decision is binding by rule rather than by accumulated work, and the node count needed for that guarantee is fixed in advance by the 3f+1 bound.

**How it works, in order.**
1. *Client request.* The client sends its transaction to the leader of the current view.
2. *Pre-prepare.* The leader orders the requests it received into a total order and broadcasts a pre-prepare message carrying the sequence number and the request digest.
3. *Prepare round.* Every replica broadcasts a prepare vote for that sequence number and waits until it holds 2f+1 prepare votes for the same proposal.
4. *Commit round.* On collecting 2f+1 matching prepares, each replica broadcasts a commit vote, and a replica executes the request only after it holds 2f+1 commit votes.
5. *Execute and reply.* The request is executed in the agreed order and the reply goes back to the client. The decision is final and cannot be rolled back.
6. *View change.* If the leader is faulty or silent, a timeout causes a new view with a different leader, so the protocol still terminates despite a Byzantine leader.

**The node-count bound, and why it holds.** The deployment must have at least 3f+1 replicas in total, and each round needs a quorum of 2f+1. The arithmetic is the whole safety proof: with 3f+1 replicas, any two quorums of 2f+1 must overlap in at least one honest replica - because two disjoint quorums would need 4f+2 replicas, which is more than exist. That honest replica can never vote for two conflicting proposals, so two conflicting blocks can never both gather 2f+1 commits.

**The worked computation.** To tolerate f faulty nodes you need 3f+1 nodes: f = 1 needs 4 nodes, f = 10 needs 31, and f = 33 needs 100. The quorum in each round is 2f+1, so with 4 nodes a commit needs 3 agreeing votes - enough that one liar, who can only reach 2 votes, cannot reach quorum alone. With 31 nodes, 21 votes are needed and 11 liars cannot supply them.

**The finality guarantee.** Once committed, the decision is final and cannot be rolled back. A permissioned chain therefore gets deterministic finality in seconds, rather than the probabilistic finality in minutes that a proof-based chain gives. For a business settling a trade, that difference is the entire commercial argument.

**Limitations.** Each transaction costs several network rounds of voting, so throughput is much lower than a probabilistic chain and the message count grows with the square of the membership size - tens of nodes, not thousands. There is no block reward, so the economics are organisational rather than incentive-based.

**Consequence.** SBFT is the mechanism behind most enterprise and consortium ledgers precisely because it converts finality from a probability into a rule, and because the known membership makes the identity and admission questions tractable for regulated institutions.

advantages: It is the simplest possible mechanism to explain and to verify: check one hash against one target.
The reward it generates is the security budget itself, so miners are paid exactly in proportion to the work they contribute to securing the chain.
The halving schedule caps total supply at 21 million BTC without requiring any authority to enforce the cap.
The difficulty adjustment keeps block times stable through hardware improvements, so the schedule does not need to be re-tweaked by governance.
limitations: Energy is destroyed every block, and the security budget per block is enormous relative to the value it protects.
Mining power has become concentrated in specialist industrial operations and in rented hash power, weakening the decentralisation argument.
Once the subsidy ends, the security budget depends entirely on transaction fees - which are volatile and could fall below what an attack costs.
The pool-and-miner structure concentrates voting power in the hands of a few pools.
The difficulty adjustment lags: a large drop in hash power produces a period of fast blocks and unstable issuance before the retarget corrects it.
Mining.memoryTrick: **Mining = double SHA-256, nonce, target. Subsidy 50 / 2^n every 210,000 blocks - then fees must pay.**
Mining.modernNote: Bitcoin's subsidy has halved six times since 2012, and mining is now dominated by industrial farms. The fee-funded endgame the syllabus describes has not arrived - the subsidy still dominates Bitcoin's security budget - but it is the structural pressure every public chain faces, and the reason proof-of-stake networks issue rewards differently.

examAnswer.question: Explain mining: the double-SHA-256 nonce search, the block subsidy halving schedule and the transition to fee-funded security. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** Mining is the activity of repeatedly hashing candidate Bitcoin block headers with varying nonces until the double SHA-256 digest falls below the network target, earning the block subsidy and fees for the block that extends the chain.

**The problem it solves.** Somebody has to pay for the security of the ledger. Mining is both the mechanism that produces blocks and the mechanism that funds the network: the subsidy it earns is the budget that pays honest miners to keep hashing and validating. It is also what makes the supply schedule enforceable without any authority - the 21 million cap is a property of the reward function, not a decree.

**How it works, in order.**
1. *Header construction.* The miner assembles the transactions into a block and writes the 80-byte header, including the previous block hash, the transaction Merkle root, a timestamp, the compact target nBits and a 32-bit nonce field it is free to set.
2. *Double hashing.* The mining hash is SHA-256 applied twice to the header - a legacy quirk inherited from Satoshi Nakamoto's original client, kept for compatibility.
3. *Nonce sweep.* The miner sets the nonce, hashes, and compares the digest with the target. If the digest is above the target, the nonce is incremented and the header hashed again, repeated until the digest falls below the target. Against a 64-bit target this needs roughly 2^64 hashes on average.
4. *Nonce exhaustion.* The nonce space is only 2^32 values, so once it is exhausted the miner changes the extraNonce inside the coinbase transaction and starts a fresh sweep.
5. *Difficulty and retargeting.* The target is reset every 2016 blocks from the actual block times so the average stays near 10 minutes per block. Difficulty is the ratio between the easiest possible target and the current one, so as hardware improves the target falls and difficulty rises.
6. *Subsidy halving.* The block reward starts at 50 BTC and halves every 210,000 blocks, so after n halvings the subsidy is 50 / 2^n BTC.
7. *Fee-funded security.* When the subsidy reaches zero, the security budget must be paid entirely by transaction fees.

**The halving schedule, with the numbers.** 50 BTC at block 0; 25 BTC from block 210,000; 12.5 BTC from block 420,000; 6.25 BTC from block 630,000; 3.125 BTC from block 840,000; and so on, halving to 1.5625 BTC and 0.78125 BTC in later periods. The general formula is the one the MCQ wants: after n halvings the subsidy is 50 / 2^n BTC. Since 210,000 blocks at 10 minutes each is 2,100,000 minutes, or about 1,458 days - roughly four years - each halving arrives about every four years. Because the subsidy halves geometrically and never becomes negative, total supply converges on 21 million BTC.

**The transition to fee-funded security.** The subsidy is a countdown. Every halving cuts the security budget that miners earn, and at some point it reaches zero, at which point the entire security of the chain must be funded by transaction fees. This is the structural pressure every public chain faces: the reward that buys security has to come from somewhere other than new issuance, and fees are volatile, so the fee market has to produce a stable enough budget to keep the cost of a 51% attack above the value at risk.

**Limitations.** Energy is destroyed every block at an enormous cost relative to the value protected; mining has concentrated in industrial farms and rented hash power; pool concentration concentrates voting power; and the difficulty adjustment lags, so a sharp fall in hash power produces a period of fast blocks and unstable issuance before the retarget corrects it.

**Consequence.** Mining is where the economics and the security of a public chain meet. The halving schedule is a promise about the money supply; the subsidy is a promise about who pays for the ledger's safety. The exam's point in every part of this question is that the second promise eventually has to be kept by the fee market.
